### Overall Assessment: Useful with Caveats

Truwit and Ronfeldt ask whether the good outcomes attributed to teacher residencies come from the model or from the programs that happen to adopt it, and they answer with the right design: a staggered-adoption difference-in-differences across 66 Tennessee preparation programs, identified off the 15 traditional (mostly undergraduate) programs that reported becoming residencies between 2011 and 2019, with program fixed effects removing the cross-program confounding that every prior residency study leaves in the estimate. On that question this is now the best-identified evidence available, and its most defensible message is a negative one: when an existing traditional program adopts the residency label and a partial bundle of its features, its graduates do not become more racially diverse and do not stay in teaching longer — nulls precise enough to rule out the large effects reported for boutique residencies. The field should weigh the paper's affirmative findings very differently. The abstract's two positive claims — that adoption may raise instructional effectiveness and increase school and district mobility — rest on one marginally significant ELA value-added coefficient (0.031, p = .084) and a school-mobility estimate (0.026, p = .020) that are precisely the two outcomes whose own parallel-trends tests are flagged (p = .079 and p = .010); the mobility result loses significance under conventional two-way fixed effects, and the diversity null carries an undiscussed pre-trend rejection of its own (p = .022). Identification comes from 15 treated clusters with no few-cluster inference correction, the treatment date is a 2019–20 recollection, and the estimand is the effect of a modest relabeling (roughly +96 required clinical hours against the ~500 a true semester-to-year shift implies) rather than of the residency model as practiced by Memphis or Boston — the 13 always-residency programs, including every externally certified one, contribute nothing. Add several text–table contradictions that survived production, a set of affirmative results reported only in prose, and no data-availability statement, code, software, or survey instrument, and the right posture is clear: cite the paper for its design and for its nulls, quote the positive estimates only with their diagnostics attached, and treat "lower bound" as the authors' interpretation rather than a demonstrated property. This sits at the upper end of "useful with caveats" — the design contribution and the retention null would be solid on their own; it is the paper's own headline positives that need qualification beyond ordinary scholarly caveats.

#### Key Strengths

- **The right design for a question the field had been answering the wrong way.** Within-program staggered DiD with program and cohort-year fixed effects removes the program-level confounders (selectivity, location, cost, faculty, reputation) that every prior residency-versus-non-residency comparison leaves in. The estimator choice (Borusyak et al. 2024) is well reasoned, the three-estimator comparison in Table A3 is transparent, and the authors headline the more conservative estimates.
- **A serious "first stage" for a self-reported treatment.** Table 2 shows that reported adoption coincides with real programmatic change — district-needs recruitment priority +23.7 pp (p < .001), yearlong placement +5.9 pp, financial incentives +6.5 pp — and Panel B corroborates it with independently reported Title II data (+95.9 required clinical hours, p = .007). Few education-policy papers with a survey-based treatment do this.
- **Informative nulls on the two outcomes that carry the policy case for residencies.** Leaving teaching: 0.005 (SE 0.009) on a ~10% base, with a clean pre-trend test (p = .284), stable across estimators and specifications. Candidate diversity: −0.013 (SE 0.010) on a ~7% base. Both intervals exclude the effect sizes single-program studies have attributed to the model.
- **Candor and a genuinely balanced literature review.** The paper foregrounds the multi-program evidence that cuts against residency advocacy, names its own 15-program identifying sample and the exclusion of all 13 always-residencies repeatedly, and pre-announces its p < .1 convention rather than smuggling it in. Table A2's cohort-composition checks support the reading that any effects run through preparation rather than recruitment.
- **Auditable sample accounting.** Every analytic N in Tables 2, 3, and A2–A4 reconciles exactly with Table 1 minus the always-residency column, and nearly every number quoted in the prose checks against its table.

#### Key Concerns

- **The abstract's affirmative claims sit on the paper's weakest diagnostics.** Instructional effectiveness rests on ELA VAM alone (math VAM and observation ratings are null under the preferred estimator), with a marginal pre-trend Wald test (p = .079) and only ~500 post-transition first-year observations; school mobility has a rejected pre-trend (p = .010) and is not significant under traditional TWFE (Table A3). Meanwhile the diversity null — the abstract's lead claim — has its own Wald rejection (F51 = 2.745, p = .022) that appears in the Table 3 row label and is never discussed in the text.
- **Inference is optimistic for the number of treated clusters.** All identifying variation comes from 15 programs; standard errors are conventional cluster-robust with no wild-cluster bootstrap or randomization inference, the paper adopts a p < .1 convention, and no multiplicity adjustment is applied across roughly 40 reported tests. The special-education result (+2.9 pp, p = .019) is one of five subject-area splits and appears only in running text. Every affirmative p-value in the paper lies between .019 and .097 — exactly where few-cluster corrections bite.
- **The estimand is a diluted relabeling, and the "lower bound" defense is asserted, asymmetric, and partly contradicted.** Treatment counts "partially" a residency as treated, moves the hallmark yearlong-placement feature only 5.9 pp, and excludes every always-residency program (which Table 1 shows have the most diverse cohorts and strongest outcomes). The lower-bound argument is invoked to shield the nulls but would equally attenuate the positives, and Table A4 shows the effectiveness estimates are driven by later — by the authors' own account, less faithful — adopters.
- **Text–table contradictions and prose-only results survived production.** The earlier/later adopter split is N = 9/6 in the text, N = 6/9 in the Table A4 note, and "six programs adopting in 2013–14 and 2014–15" one sentence later. Observation ratings average "23 rubric items" in Methods but the Discussion's effect-size benchmark uses 15. Table 1's In-state total (22,384) does not equal its column sum (22,304). The special-education effect, the partner-district mobility subgroup analysis (which conditions on a post-treatment outcome), the school-characteristic difference scores, and the controls sensitivity check have no exhibit at all.
- **No independent verification path.** There is no data-availability statement, no replication package, no named software or estimation routine, and the treatment variable comes from an unpublished survey instrument. The Wald tests are printed with a single degrees-of-freedom subscript that cannot reproduce the p-values, Column 2 of Table 3 has no pre-trend diagnostics, and the Title II merge convention (notes 11–12) is left unstated — so even the one public-data analysis cannot be checked.

#### What to Rely On

- **The design critique and its remedy.** Cross-program comparisons of residency and non-residency graduates cannot separate the model from the program; within-program staggered DiD on dated adoption, with a documented first stage, is a workable alternative. This is the paper's most transferable contribution and the safest thing to cite it for.
- **What "becoming a residency" actually meant in practice.** Table 2 is the best available evidence that self-described residency adoption at scale is a modest bundle — mostly a stronger recruitment orientation toward district staffing needs plus roughly 96 extra required clinical hours — not a wholesale conversion to the model.
- **The retention null.** Adoption did not reduce first-year exit from teaching (0.005, SE 0.009), with a clean pre-trend test, replicated across estimators and across first-year and all-year specifications. This is the cleanest estimate in the paper.
- **The diversity null, with two caveats attached.** Adoption did not make graduating cohorts more racially diverse (−0.013, SE 0.010), consistent with the multi-program literature — but cite it alongside its p = .022 pre-trend rejection and the fact that Tennessee's candidate pool is 90.7% White and mostly undergraduate.
- **Stable cohort composition across the transition (Table A2).** No detectable change in gender, elementary endorsement, in-state residence, prior teaching experience, or prior achievement, which is the best evidence in the paper that any effects run through preparation rather than recruitment.
- **Descriptive facts about Tennessee's teacher pipeline in Table 1** — 90.7% White completers, 58.7% employed in-state within a year, 10.6% first-year attrition — which are straightforward tabulations of statewide administrative data.

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- **"Adoption may increase instructional effectiveness."** One marginal ELA VAM coefficient (p = .084) with a marginal pre-trend test (p = .079), null math VAM and observation ratings, roughly 500 post-transition observations, and — per Table A4 — effects concentrated among the least-faithful adopters. A hypothesis, not a finding; quote the coefficient and its diagnostics, never the abstract sentence alone.
- **"Adoption increases school and district mobility."** The school-mobility estimate has a rejected parallel-trends test (p = .010), loses significance under traditional TWFE, and Column 2's tighter standard errors come from stacking teacher-years within the same 15 treated programs, not from more identifying variation. District mobility (p = .097, clean pre-trend) is the better-supported of the two, and only marginally.
- **The partner-district mobility reversal (−2.3 pp, p = .004).** It conditions on partner-district employment — itself an outcome of treatment — is reported with no table, standard errors, or Ns, and partner districts are defined retroactively from a 2020 mandate. A collider-prone descriptive contrast, not the causal reassurance the Discussion presents it as.
- **The special-education endorsement effect (+2.9 pp, p = .019).** One of five unadjusted subject-area splits, prose-only with no SE or N, and carrying a 14.2% baseline that is essentially identical to the 14.4% all-high-need baseline — a discrepancy the paper never explains. The aggregate high-need estimate is p = .233.
- **The employment and partner-district-employment nulls.** These are imprecise, not tight: partner-district employment (0.025, SE 0.019) cannot rule out a ~6 pp increase on a 26% base, and ever-employed (0.011, SE 0.022) is essentially uninformative. Do not cite them as evidence that the model cannot redistribute teachers.
- **"Our estimates are lower bounds for the full model."** Asserted four times, never bounded, applied only to defend nulls, and in tension with Table A4. Attenuation from mis-dated treatment under an imputation estimator is not necessarily toward zero.
- **Anything in Table A4.** The text and the table note contradict each other on which cohort has 6 programs and which has 9, and a later-adopter ELA VAM of 0.080 with SE 0.009 (t ≈ 9) from at most nine treated programs is not a credible level of precision.
- **The observation-rating effect-size benchmark ("half a point on 1 of 15 indicators").** Methods says 23 rubric items; the benchmark only works with 15. Use the raw estimate (0.032 on a five-point scale, not significant) instead.
- **"Some of the strongest evidence yet" and "it may pay dividends in elevating early-career teaching quality."** Read the first as a claim about identification, not evidentiary weight; treat the second — the sentence most likely to be lifted into a policy brief — as the least supported sentence in the paper.

### Methods Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The paper applies a modern, heterogeneity-robust staggered-adoption DiD estimator (Borusyak, Jaravel & Spiess, 2024) to a genuinely novel data linkage — a retrospective 2019-20 census-like survey of Tennessee preparation programs merged to statewide administrative graduate, personnel, and evaluation records — and is unusually candid about its own limits. But the entire causal payload rests on 15 treated programs whose treatment date is self-recalled up to eight years after the fact, inference is conventional cluster-robust with few treated clusters and no wild-cluster bootstrap, and the two headline positive findings (school mobility, ELA value-added) sit on outcomes whose own parallel-trends Wald tests are rejected or marginal. Readers should treat the design as an honest and valuable improvement on prior residency research and the individual point estimates as suggestive rather than settled.

**Strengths:**

- The core design choice is the right one for the question. Prior residency research compares residency graduates to non-residency graduates in the same districts, which cannot separate the model from everything else that differs across programs (selectivity, location, cost, faculty, reputation). Program and cohort-year fixed effects, identified off within-program transitions, directly address the confound the literature has been unable to escape. This is a real methodological advance, and the paper is explicit that it buys internal validity at the price of generalizing only to programs that transitioned.
- Estimator selection is well-reasoned rather than mechanical. The authors explain why classical TWFE is risky here (staggered timing plus plausibly dynamic and cohort-heterogeneous effects), justify the BJS imputation estimator on three concrete grounds (robustness to anticipation, pre-trend testing using only untreated observations, suitability for individual-level data under a group-level treatment), and Note 9 correctly flags the trade-off — using the whole pre-period as baseline gains precision but imposes a stronger parallel-trends assumption. Note 9 also documents a useful check: identical estimates and SEs when collapsing to a program-by-year pseudo-panel with cell-size weights.
- Treatment validation is more serious than in most survey-based DiD work. Table 2 Panel A runs the same DiD with seven self-reported model features as outcomes and finds theoretically coherent effects (district-needs recruitment priority +23.7 pp, p < .001; yearlong clinical placement +5.9 pp, p < .001; mentor compensation +4.5 pp, p = .005; financial incentives +6.5 pp, p < .001). Panel B then goes outside the survey to federally reported Title II data and finds +95.9 hours (SE 35.67, p = .007) of required supervised clinical experience — an independent, non-retrospective corroboration that the self-reported transition marks a real programmatic change.
- Right-censoring is recognized and handled sensibly. Because earlier graduates mechanically have more years at risk of employment, exit, mobility, and experience-driven effectiveness gains, the preferred specification restricts to the single post-graduation year observable for every cohort, with all-years models reported alongside. Note 7 lays out precisely why censoring threatens the interpretation of dynamic pre- and post-trends, not just levels.
- Cohort-composition balance tests (Table A2) show no detectable effects on gender, elementary endorsement, in-state residence, prior teaching experience, or standardized prior academic achievement, which supports the paper's central interpretive move — that whatever effects appear are more likely to run through preparation than through changes in who enrolls.
- Estimator sensitivity is reported transparently (Table A3), and the authors deliberately present the most conservative of the three sets of estimates as headline. The de Chaisemartin–D'Haultfoeuille alternative yields uniformly larger effects (math VAM 0.096, p < .01; moved districts 0.037, p < .01), so the paper is not cherry-picking the specification that flatters its story.
- Sample-representativeness is checked rather than asserted: a 72.9% program response rate covering 84.2% of graduates, plus Table A1 regressions of characteristics and outcomes on survey response showing broad comparability apart from an undergraduate/graduate imbalance.

**Weaknesses:**

- Inference with few treated clusters is not addressed. All identifying variation comes from 15 treated programs; standard errors are ordinary cluster-robust at the program level (Wald test dfs of 42-51 indicate roughly 43-52 usable clusters). With this few treated clusters, cluster-robust SEs are well known to be downward-biased and t-tests to over-reject. No wild cluster bootstrap, randomization inference, or few-treated-cluster correction is reported anywhere. This matters most for exactly the estimates the paper leans on, all of which are borderline: moved schools 0.026 (0.011), p = .020; moved districts 0.012 (0.008), p = .097; ELA VAM 0.031 (0.018), p = .084; special education endorsements 2.9 pp, p = .019. The paper's stated response to imprecision — adopting p < .1 as "marginally significant" — pushes in the opposite direction from what few-treated-cluster inference would counsel.
- The two significant positive first-year findings sit on outcomes with flagged pre-trends. School mobility (0.026*, the largest conventionally significant effect in Table 3) has a rejected parallel-trends test, F(48) = 3.186, p = .010; ELA value-added (0.031+) has F(42) = 2.145, p = .079. The paper flags both in the text, to its credit, but then still features them in the abstract and discussion as the study's affirmative contributions. Of the outcomes reaching any conventional threshold in the preferred first-year specification, only "moved districts" (p = .097, Wald p = .241) combines statistical significance with a clean pre-trend test.
- The parallel-trends violation on candidate diversity is never discussed. Table 3 reports F(51) = 2.745, p = .022 for candidate diversity — a rejection at the 5% level — yet the results text discusses only the mobility (p = .010) and ELA VAM (p = .079) Wald tests. The paper's single most policy-salient claim, and the first item in the abstract's "we generate skepticism" sentence, is the null on teacher diversity (−0.013, SE 0.010). That null rests on an outcome for which the design's key identifying assumption is statistically rejected, and Table 1 shows adopters' minority share falling from 0.07 pre to 0.05 post, consistent with a differential downward trajectory that may predate adoption.
- The retrospective, self-reported treatment date is the design's weakest link, and the paper's characterization of its consequences is too benign. Program leaders in 2019-20 were asked to recall the school year in which their program "began to consider" itself a residency, for transitions occurring as far back as 2011. The authors treat the resulting error as classical and therefore attenuating, warranting a "lower bound" reading. But recall error in treatment timing under an imputation estimator is not classical: mis-timed units contaminate the untreated pool from which counterfactuals are fit, and recall is plausibly anchored to salient or outcome-correlated events (the state's district-partnership mandate, a favorable report-card year), which can generate spurious effects rather than attenuate real ones. The paper's own evidence points this way: Table 2/Figure 1 show programs adopting district partnerships and mentor training in the years before their self-reported transition date (Wald p = .013 and p = .001), i.e., treatment timing recorded later than actual programmatic change.
- The "lower bound" framing is applied asymmetrically and does not hold for the paper's negative results. Attenuation and low power make it easier to fail to reject a null, so the same forces the authors invoke to argue their positive estimates understate true effects also make their headline nulls — no effect on diversity, employment, or retention — easier to obtain for reasons unrelated to the model's true efficacy. The discussion acknowledges the power problem, but the abstract's claim to "generate skepticism" about diversity, employment, and retention improvements is stated more strongly than the evidence permits.
- Several nulls are not precise enough to sustain the claims built on them. Partner-district employment is 0.025 (SE 0.019) against a pre-period base of 0.26 — the confidence interval comfortably includes a 6 pp (roughly 23% relative) increase, so the discussion's suggestion of "limits to the potential of the model to redistribute teachers to specific district settings" is not supported by a tight null. Ever-employed is 0.011 (SE 0.022) on a base of 0.54: essentially uninformative. By contrast, the leaving-teaching null (0.005, SE 0.009, base 0.09-0.11) and the diversity null are reasonably tight in absolute terms — the paper does not distinguish among these cases.
- All retention, mobility, and effectiveness outcomes condition on post-treatment employment, and the partner-district subgroup analysis conditions on an outcome the treatment may itself move. Mobility outcomes are estimated on the employed (N = 12,812 vs 22,099) and, for school/district moves, on the employed-and-retained (N = 11,454). The exploratory finding that adoption reduces district mobility among graduates employed in partner districts (−2.3 pp, p = .004 first year; −1.2 pp, p < .001 all years) and that this differs from the effect among graduates elsewhere (p < .001 and p = .012) splits the sample on partner-district employment — itself an estimated outcome of treatment (+0.025 in Table 3). These are collider-prone comparisons, not causal contrasts, and no selection bounds (e.g., Lee bounds) are reported. None of these subgroup estimates appear in a table.
- Coding "partially" a residency as fully treated makes the treatment a diffuse bundle. The paper's own validation quantifies how diffuse: adoption raises the probability of reporting a yearlong clinical placement — the model's hallmark feature — by only 5.9 pp, and raises required clinical hours by 95.9 rather than the ~500 the authors note a semester-to-year shift would imply. The estimates are therefore effects of a modest average change in practice, not of the residency model as conventionally described, and the "lower bound for full implementation" extrapolation is an assumption rather than something the data test.
- Multiplicity is unaddressed across a large number of tests. The paper reports 10 primary outcomes in two specifications, 9 treatment-validation outcomes, 5 balance tests, 5 endorsement-subject disaggregations, adoption-cohort splits, partner-district subgroup contrasts, and a set of school-characteristic difference scores. Its cleanest recruitment result — special education endorsements, +2.9 pp, p = .019 — is one of five subject-area disaggregations and no correction is applied. That estimate also appears only in running text: no standard error, no N, and no parallel-trends test are reported for it anywhere.
- Table A4 and the text contradict each other on the adoption-cohort split. The text describes "earlier (up through 2015–2016, N = 9) and later-adopting (in 2016–2017 or after, N = 6)" and then discusses "the six programs adopting the model in the 2013–2014 and 2014–2015 school years"; the Table A4 note states "Earlier adopters are those (N = 6) who adopted... prior to the 2016–2017 school year; later adopters are those (N = 9) who adopted in 2016–2017 or after." The observation counts (earlier column 21,155 vs later 17,777 of 21,956 total) imply earlier-adopting programs contribute roughly five times as many observations, favoring the text's assignment, but readers cannot resolve which group is which from the paper alone. This split also produces implausibly precise estimates — later adopters' ELA VAM of 0.080 with SE 0.009 (t ≈ 8.9) from at most nine treated programs — which should be read as an artifact of few-cluster inference rather than a finding.
- Two data-construction choices deserve more scrutiny than they receive. Partner districts are defined from partnerships that existed by the 2020 state mandate and applied retroactively to all earlier years (Note 4), so the partner-district employment and partner-district mobility outcomes are anachronistically measured for early cohorts — a particular problem given the paper's own argument that partnership formation was a response to that mandate. And observation-rating coverage varies substantially by cohort (75.7% of employed 2016-17 completers vs 93.2% of 2017-18 completers, Note 5); year fixed effects absorb only the common component of that variation.
- SUTVA is not discussed. Fifteen treated and 34 never-treated programs compete in a single state teacher labor market. If residency adoption improves treated graduates' access to jobs in partner districts, comparison programs' graduates may be displaced, biasing employment and mobility estimates away from zero; conversely, the documented diffusion of residency features to non-adopters (the paper notes non-residencies were extending their own placements) contaminates the control group toward zero. Neither direction is bounded or bracketed.
- The all-years (Column 2) estimates should not be read as independent confirmation. Their much tighter standard errors (moved schools 0.018 with SE 0.004; moved districts 0.009 with SE 0.003) come from stacking repeated teacher-year observations within the same 66 programs; the number of independent treated units remains 15. The three-star significance in that column reflects observation count, not additional identifying variation.
- Effect magnitudes rest in places on thin cells. The value-added results — the paper's most touted positive finding — use first-year samples of 2,400 (math) and 2,613 (ELA), of which post-transition observations number roughly 436 and 507 spread across 15 programs, in a series with no 2019-20 data and severely degraded 2015-16 coverage. No event-study coefficients are reported numerically anywhere, so readers cannot inspect the dynamic patterns the paper repeatedly invokes as corroborating "face validity."

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Read the paper as strong evidence about a research design and weak-to-moderate evidence about any individual coefficient. Its durable contribution is the demonstration that within-program transitions can be used to strip out program-level confounding in residency research; no single estimate in Table 3 should be cited as an established magnitude.
- Treat the null on teacher diversity as "no evidence of improvement," not "evidence of no effect," and note when citing it that its own parallel-trends test is rejected (F(51) = 2.745, p = .022) — the only Table 3 Wald rejection the results text does not discuss. Anyone building on the claim that residency adoption fails to diversify graduating cohorts should verify it against a design that does not depend on this outcome's pre-trend holding.
- Do not cite the school-mobility finding (+2.6 pp, p = .020) as a clean causal effect. Its parallel-trends test fails at p = .010, and the paper's own evidence that programs adopt model features one to two years before self-reporting a transition means the flagged pre-trend is equally consistent with genuinely earlier treatment or with confounding — the design cannot distinguish these. The district-mobility estimate (+1.2 pp, p = .097, Wald p = .241) is the better-supported of the two mobility results, but only marginally significant.
- Discount the marginal p-values by at least one notch for few-treated-cluster inference. Fifteen treated clusters with conventional cluster-robust SEs and no wild bootstrap means the reported p-values of .019, .020, .079, .084, and .097 are likely optimistic. Before building on any of these, ask whether the finding would survive randomization inference.
- Read the effectiveness results as the study's most interesting but least secure finding. All three point estimates are positive and mutually consistent (ORs +0.032; math VAM +0.034; ELA VAM +0.031), which is genuine circumstantial support, but only ELA is marginally significant, its pre-trend test is marginal (p = .079), and it rests on ~500 post-transition first-year observations. The paper's benchmark — roughly half the average first-to-second-year experience gain — is a fair characterization of the point estimate, not of the lower end of its interval.
- Ignore the adoption-cohort heterogeneity in Table A4 for substantive purposes. The table's note contradicts the text about which group has 9 programs and which has 6, and the later-adopter estimates (ELA VAM 0.080 with SE 0.009) are too precise to be credible from that few clusters. Do not cite "later adopters drive the VAM effect" as a finding.
- Treat the partner-district mobility subgroup results (−2.3 pp, p = .004; −1.2 pp, p < .001) as descriptive, not causal. They condition on partner-district employment, which the same paper estimates as a (statistically insignificant) outcome of treatment, so the subgroup contrast is a comparison of endogenously selected groups. The reassuring conclusion built on them — that increased mobility does not pull graduates out of partner districts — is a plausible conjecture, not an identified result.
- Interpret "lower bound" only for effects the paper finds to be positive, and never for its nulls. The attenuation and diffuse-treatment arguments that justify reading positive estimates as understated also make the null results easier to obtain, so the abstract's skepticism about diversity, employment, and retention gains is not itself shielded by that framing.
- When citing the employment nulls, quote the interval rather than the point estimate. Partner-district employment (0.025, SE 0.019) cannot rule out a roughly 6 pp increase on a 26% base, and ever-employed (0.011, SE 0.022) is essentially uninformative. The retention null (0.005, SE 0.009 on a ~10% base) is the tightest of the three and the only one that supports a genuine "no meaningful effect" reading.
- Remember what "treatment" is here. The paper's own validation shows adoption raised the reported yearlong-placement rate by only 5.9 pp and required clinical hours by 95.9 (against roughly 500 for a semester-to-year shift), with "partially" counted as treated. These are effects of a modest, heterogeneous bundle of programmatic changes at previously traditional, mostly undergraduate programs — not effects of the residency model as implemented by Memphis or Nashville Teacher Residency, which the design excludes by construction.
- Do not extend these estimates to graduate-level or purpose-built residencies. The 13 always-residency programs — including all seven externally certified by NCTR or the state, and the ones Table 1 shows with the strongest graduate outcomes — contribute nothing to identification. The paper says this clearly; readers should carry the caveat forward.
- Before building on the partner-district employment and mobility outcomes, note that partnerships are defined from the 2020 state mandate and applied retroactively to all prior years (Note 4). For early cohorts these variables measure membership in a partnership that did not yet exist.
- Anyone attempting to replicate or extend this should ask the authors for numeric event-study coefficients (reported only graphically), the standard error and N behind the special-education estimate (text only), and the subgroup mobility estimates (text only). Independent re-verification of treatment timing against Title II or state accreditation records would be the single highest-value robustness check, since the retrospective survey date is the design's load-bearing measurement.

**Detailed Commentary:**

What the design does well, and what it costs. The identification idea is sound and well-matched to the gap in the literature. Prior residency evaluations compare residency graduates to other novices in the same districts and therefore cannot rule out that any advantage reflects program selectivity, location, cost, reputation, or candidate sorting rather than the model. Program and cohort-year fixed effects, with treatment defined as a program's own transition, address that confound head-on. The cost is stated honestly: with program fixed effects, only programs that switch contribute, so 13 always-residency programs — including every externally certified one and, per Table 1, those with the strongest raw outcomes — drop out entirely, and 4 programs adopting in 2019-20 are observed only pre-transition. Identification therefore comes from 15 mostly undergraduate programs, and the estimand is "what happens when a traditional undergraduate program partially adopts residency features," not "what a well-implemented residency does."

Estimator and inference. The BJS imputation estimator is a defensible choice given staggered timing and plausible dynamic and cohort heterogeneity, and Note 9 shows the authors understand its properties, including the stronger parallel-trends requirement that comes with using the whole pre-period as baseline and the resulting change in how a pre-trend violation looks (a nonzero slope from near zero, not a series ending at zero at t−1). Table A3's three-estimator comparison is genuinely reassuring on direction and rough magnitude, and presenting the most conservative set as headline is the right call. The gap is inference, not estimation. With 15 treated clusters, cluster-robust standard errors are known to be biased downward and to over-reject; nothing in the paper corrects for this. Every affirmative finding lives between p = .019 and p = .097, precisely the region where a few-treated-cluster correction typically bites. The paper's response to imprecision — treating p < .1 as marginally significant and leaning on the visual face validity of event studies whose coefficients are never tabulated — moves in the opposite direction from what the cluster structure warrants.

Parallel trends, outcome by outcome. Table 3 reports a cluster-robust Wald test per outcome, which is good practice and lets a reader audit the paper's claims. Doing so: clean tests accompany high-need endorsements (p = .557), ever-employed (p = .275), partner-district employment (p = .971), left teaching (p = .284), moved districts (p = .241), observation ratings (p = .668), and math VAM (p = .198) — all of which are statistically insignificant. Rejections or near-rejections accompany candidate diversity (p = .022), moved schools (p = .010), and ELA VAM (p = .079) — which are, respectively, the paper's headline null and its two significant positive results. That correlation between failed pre-trend tests and reported findings is the central thing a reader needs to carry away. The paper discusses two of the three; the diversity rejection at p = .022 goes unmentioned in the results text despite anchoring the abstract's skepticism claim and despite Table 1 showing adopters' minority share declining from 0.07 pre to 0.05 post. The same pattern recurs in Table 2: the two features showing no adoption effect (district partnership, mentor training) are exactly the two with rejected pre-trends (p = .013, p = .001), which the authors read as anticipation.

The anticipation reading cuts both ways. The authors argue, reasonably, that programs implemented partnerships and mentor training before self-identifying as residencies, so the self-reported transition date is late relative to real programmatic change. If so, pre-period observations for treated programs are already partially treated. That contaminates the counterfactual the imputation estimator fits and simultaneously offers an alternative, benign explanation for the flagged outcome pre-trends. The design cannot separate "early treatment" from "differential trend," so a reader confronting the mobility pre-trend violation should hold both readings open rather than accepting either.

Measurement of treatment. A 2019-20 survey asking leaders to recall the year their program became a residency — for transitions dating to 2011, at institutions with administrative turnover — is a serious measurement problem, and the authors deserve credit for anticipating it, mitigating it (encouraging collaborative response), and validating it against features and Title II hours. The Title II corroboration (+95.9 hours, p = .007) is the strongest single piece of evidence that the self-reported transitions are real. What is too quick is the inference that the resulting error is classical and therefore attenuating. Under an imputation estimator, units with mis-dated onset both lose treated observations and pollute the untreated pool used to fit counterfactuals, and recall is plausibly anchored to salient institutional events — the state partnership mandate, a favorable report-card year — that may correlate with the outcomes. The direction of bias is not pinned down, and non-classical recall anchored to outcome improvements would produce spurious positive effects.

Post-treatment conditioning. Everything in Panels C and D is estimated on the employed (N = 12,812 of 22,099), and school/district moves additionally on the retained (N = 11,454). The employment effect is small and insignificant, so selection is probably modest, but it is unbounded — no Lee bounds or equivalent appear. The exploratory partner-district mobility analysis goes further, splitting on partner-district employment, which Table 3 itself treats as an outcome (+0.025). The resulting estimates (−2.3 pp, p = .004; −1.2 pp, p < .001) and the cross-subgroup difference tests (p < .001, p = .012) are collider-prone and appear in no table. The discussion nonetheless uses them to reassure readers that the mobility increase is not pulling graduates away from partner districts. That reassurance is a plausible hypothesis, not an identified result.

What the evidence firmly supports. (1) Self-reported residency adoption among these 15 programs corresponds to real, if modest, programmatic change — most clearly a longer required clinical experience (+95.9 hours from independent Title II reporting, p = .007) and a sharply higher stated recruitment priority on district staffing needs (+23.7 pp, p < .001). (2) Adoption did not produce large improvements in graduate racial diversity or in retention in teaching; the confidence intervals on those two outcomes are tight enough in absolute terms to rule out the large effects prior single-program studies suggested — with the important qualifier that the diversity outcome's pre-trend test fails. (3) Observable cohort composition is stable across the transition (Table A2), which is the best evidence in the paper that any effects run through preparation rather than recruitment. (4) The design itself: the paper demonstrates that within-program transitions plus statewide administrative data can do work that district-matched comparisons cannot.

What is fragile. (1) The instructional-effectiveness story. Three positive, mutually consistent point estimates is meaningful circumstantial evidence, but only ELA reaches marginal significance, its pre-trend test is marginal, and it rests on a few hundred post-transition observations in a series missing 2019-20 and largely missing 2015-16. (2) The mobility story. Significant but pre-trend-flagged for schools, marginal but clean for districts; the all-years column's tighter SEs add observations, not identifying variation. (3) The high-need endorsement story. The aggregate is p = .233; the special-education result (p = .019) is one of five subject-area splits with no multiplicity adjustment and is reported only in running text with no SE, N, or pre-trend test. (4) The employment nulls, which are not precise enough to support the discussion's conclusions about the model's limited ability to redistribute teachers into partner districts. (5) Anything in Table A4, where the note and text contradict each other on group sizes and where a t-statistic near 9 emerges from at most nine treated clusters.

External validity beyond what the paper says. The authors are thorough on generalizability to always-residency and graduate programs. Two threats get less attention. First, sample selection: 27.1% of programs did not respond, and Table A1 shows responders differ significantly on undergraduate/graduate composition (0.352, p < .05) and, notably, on district mobility (0.030, p < .01) — the same outcome that produces one of the paper's headline findings. Second, SUTVA. Fifteen adopters and 34 never-adopters compete in one state labor market; job displacement between them would inflate employment and mobility estimates, while the documented spread of residency features to non-adopters would deflate everything toward zero. Neither is discussed or bounded.

Bottom line for a reader. This is careful, self-aware quasi-experimental work that earns its place in the literature primarily as a design contribution and as a well-grounded corrective to the inference that boutique residencies' good outcomes are caused by the residency model. It does not establish that adoption improves instructional effectiveness, and it does not establish that adoption increases mobility. Its most defensible substantive message is negative and appropriately modest: within this set of transitions, the large diversity and retention gains reported in single-program studies do not appear, and readers should be skeptical of attributing those gains to the model itself. The positive findings are hypotheses for the next study, not conclusions.

---

### Literature Review

**Rating:** Strong (moderate confidence)

Within its core domain — evaluations of teacher residencies — this paper's literature review is close to a complete census (Papay et al. 2012; An & Koedel 2021; Silva et al. 2014/2015; Matsko et al. 2022; Terziev & Forde 2021; Wan et al. 2021; Guha et al. 2016; Perlstein et al. 2014; Sloan & Blazevski 2015; Solomon 2009; Roegman et al. 2017), and it is unusually disciplined about presenting that evidence as genuinely mixed rather than uniformly promising. The characterizations of prior findings I can check are accurate, and the discussion returns to each prior result the paper fails to replicate instead of quietly dropping it. The gaps are in adjacent literatures rather than the core: the teacher labor-market/mobility literature that would frame its most novel finding, the clinical-placement-match literature, the TPP-effect-heterogeneity literature, and the inference-side econometrics (pre-trend test power, few-treated-cluster inference) that bears directly on how much the p-values in this paper should be trusted.

**Strengths:**

- Near-complete coverage of the residency evaluation literature, including the grey/REL literature (Terziev & Forde 2021; Wan et al. 2021; Silva et al. 2014/2015; Perlstein et al. 2014; Sloan et al. 2018) that many published treatments skip. A reader looking for an entry point into "what has been studied about teacher residencies" can use this reference list as a bibliography.
- Exemplary handling of conflicting evidence. The review is organized around a real and correctly identified fault line — single-program studies find positive effects on diversity, endorsements, and retention; multi-program studies mostly do not (Matsko et al. 2022; Terziev & Forde 2021; Wan et al. 2021) — and the paper uses that pattern as a motivating puzzle rather than burying it. The discussion then walks back through each prior finding it fails to reproduce and offers competing explanations for the divergence.
- The paper's central critique of the prior literature — that residency-vs-nonresidency comparisons cannot separate the model from correlated program attributes (location, cost, reputation, faculty quality, selectivity) — is correct, clearly stated, and not overstated. It is the strongest part of the scholarly positioning.
- Candor about the scope of its own contribution: the paper repeatedly tells readers that its estimates come from only 15 mostly-undergraduate transitioning programs, that the 13 always-residency programs (including the NCTR-recognized ones most likely to implement well) contribute nothing, and that its treatment is a coarse self-report. Few papers so consistently undercut their own headline.
- Appropriate engagement with the staggered-DiD methods literature for the estimation problem it faces (Goodman-Bacon 2021; Borusyak et al. 2024; de Chaisemartin & D'Haultfoeuille 2023; Roth et al. 2023), with a stated and defensible rationale for the imputation estimator and a robustness table spanning the estimator space.

**Weaknesses:**

- The most novel finding — increased school and district mobility among residency graduates — is the least well-situated. The paper supports it only with descriptive antecedents (Roegman et al. 2017; Silva et al. 2014/2015) and then interprets it via an unsourced match-quality story ("finding a more optimal fit"). The large teacher labor-market literature that would adjudicate this reading is absent: Boyd et al. on the "draw of home" and preference-driven sorting, Hanushek/Kain/Rivkin and Feng/Sass on transition patterns, and Ronfeldt/Loeb/Wyckoff (2013) on whether turnover itself is harmful. A reader has no way, from this paper alone, to judge whether a 2.6pp mobility increase is benign sorting or churn.
- The clinical-placement literature is compressed into a single review citation (Ronfeldt 2021), which under-serves readers on the paper's own causal mechanism. Most consequentially, the Goldhaber/Krieg/Theobald line of work on student-teaching placement matching — which shows that where candidates are placed predicts where they are hired and how effective they are — speaks directly to both the partner-district employment null and the mobility finding, and is not cited.
- No engagement with the literature on how much teacher effectiveness actually varies across preparation programs (e.g., von Hippel & Bellows 2018; Koedel et al. 2015; Mihaly et al. 2013), which finds that measured cross-program differences are largely noise. This matters for reading the paper two ways: it makes small, imprecise effects the expected result rather than a disappointment, and it strengthens the paper's own "something else" framing. Its absence lets readers over-read the nulls as a verdict on residencies rather than as what an underpowered program-level design typically yields.
- The inference-side econometrics is thin relative to the estimation-side econometrics. The paper leans on cluster-robust Wald tests for parallel trends as evidence for and against causal interpretation, but does not cite the work showing these tests are badly underpowered (Roth 2022) or the sensitivity-analysis alternative (Rambachan & Roth 2023). Nor does it cite the few-clusters inference literature (Cameron/Gelbach/Miller; MacKinnon/Webb) despite identification resting on 15 treated programs. With this design, "no detected pre-trend violation" is close to uninformative, and the marginal p-values (.059–.097) that carry several conclusions are more fragile than they appear.
- Novelty is oversold in one specific sentence. The conclusion claims "some of the strongest evidence yet" on instructional effectiveness, which rests on a marginally significant ELA VAM (p = .084 / .059) whose own pre-trend Wald test is marginally significant (p = .079), alongside a null math VAM and a null observation rating. The claim is defensible as a statement about identification (this is plausibly the best-identified design on residency adoption) but not about evidentiary weight. The abstract's "suggestive evidence" is the better-calibrated phrase; readers should treat the conclusion's wording as the outlier.
- Heavy load-bearing reliance on one companion self-citation. Truwit et al. (2024) is cited roughly nine times and supplies several premises the paper's interpretation depends on — that residencies differ from traditional programs in features, that earlier adopters implemented more faithfully, that externally certified residencies implement better, that the model's distinctiveness is declining. These are reasonable, but they come from the same authors using the same survey instrument, so they are not independent corroboration.
- The paper cites institutional-isomorphism work (Reagan et al. 2021; Truwit et al. 2024) to explain why programs adopted — mimetic response to publicized report-card success of early residencies, plus a coercive state partnership mandate — but never connects that account back to its own identifying assumption. If adoption is a response to observed outcome performance, adoption is endogenous to outcome trends, which is precisely the parallel-trends threat. The two threads sit in the same paper without ever meeting.
- Guha et al. (2016), a Learning Policy Institute synthesis from an organization that advocates for the model, does substantial framing work in the introduction, abstract, and discussion as the stand-in for "what the field believes." The paper hedges ("existing, albeit limited, evidence"), but readers should register that this anchor is an advocacy-adjacent synthesis rather than an independent evaluation.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Read this alongside Papay, West, Fullerton & Kane (2012) and An & Koedel (2021) rather than as a replacement for them. Those papers answer "are residency graduates different from other novices in the same district?" (a descriptive/selection question); this paper answers "does a traditional program that converts to a residency change its graduates' outcomes?" (a within-program treatment question). They can both be right — the paper's own preferred explanation for the diversity divergence is exactly that the earlier positive findings reflect program-level correlates rather than model features.
- For the mobility finding — the paper's most surprising result and the one with the thinnest literature scaffolding — supply your own context from the teacher labor-market literature (Boyd, Lankford, Loeb & Wyckoff on proximity/preference-driven sorting; Ronfeldt, Loeb & Wyckoff 2013 on whether turnover is itself harmful). The paper's benign "better job match" reading is a hypothesis it does not test, and the exploratory follow-ups it does run (no shift toward whiter or higher-achieving schools; reduced mobility among partner-district hires) constrain the pessimistic reading but do not establish the optimistic one.
- Before repeating the paper's summary that its effectiveness estimates are "roughly consistent in size with limited prior literature (An & Koedel, 2021)," check An & Koedel's actual magnitudes. This paper's preferred math VAM estimate is 0.034 SD and null; An & Koedel's Kansas City residency estimates are, to my recollection, appreciably larger. "Consistent in sign" is safe; "consistent in size" is the claim worth verifying at the source.
- Also verify against the source before repeating: the paper's framing that evidence on residency graduates' instructional effectiveness is limited to Boston and Kansas City. The Mathematica multisite evaluation of Teacher Quality Partnership residency grantees (Silva et al. 2014) reported student-achievement comparisons across sites, and the paper cites it only for endorsement, diversity, and retention outcomes. If that report contains additional (and I believe largely null or mixed) achievement results, the effectiveness evidence base is somewhat less sparse and somewhat less favorable than this review implies. Similarly, Terziev & Forde (2021) is an early-implementation study; treat its "no diversity difference" finding as descriptive implementation evidence, not an outcome evaluation.
- Read the conclusion's "strongest evidence yet" as a claim about research design, not about statistical strength. The correct citation of this paper is for its identification strategy (first staggered-adoption DiD on residency conversion, with a survey-based treatment corroborated against Title II clinical-hours data) and for its well-powered nulls on diversity and retention — not as positive evidence that residencies raise effectiveness. That conclusion rests on one marginal ELA VAM coefficient with a marginal pre-trend test.
- Treat every parallel-trends verdict in this paper as low-information in both directions. With 15 treated clusters, the Wald tests reported under each outcome in Tables 2 and 3 have little power to detect real violations (Roth 2022), so passing one is weak reassurance — and the ones that fail (school mobility, ELA VAM) sit under two of the paper's three positive findings. Rambachan & Roth (2023) sensitivity bounds are the modern way to bound this; the paper does not report them, so readers should widen their own uncertainty accordingly.
- Note that the treatment here is not "the residency model" as the Boston or Memphis programs practice it. It is whatever 15 mostly-undergraduate Tennessee programs did when they began calling themselves at least "partially" residencies — validated as roughly +96 clinical hours against a full-model benchmark the paper itself estimates at ~500. The paper says this plainly and calls its estimates lower bounds; readers should carry that qualifier into any citation, and should not read the diversity and retention nulls as evidence about well-implemented residencies.
- For readers coming to this from outside teacher education: the intellectual antecedent the paper does not cite but clearly descends from is Boyd, Grossman, Lankford, Loeb & Wyckoff (2009, EEPA) on preparation features rather than pathway labels predicting first-year effectiveness. Pairing that paper's feature-level framing with this one's within-program design gives a much fuller picture of the "model itself or something else" question than either alone.
- The five features-of-the-model premises the paper relies on (that residencies differ in features, that earlier adopters implemented more faithfully, that externally certified residencies implement better, that model distinctiveness is declining) all trace to Truwit et al. (2024), the authors' own companion paper on the same survey. Read that paper if you intend to lean on any of these premises independently; do not treat them as externally replicated.

**Detailed Commentary:**

Transparency about my own limits: I know the teacher preparation, teacher labor market, and staggered-DiD econometrics literatures reasonably well, and I am fairly confident about the content of Papay et al. (2012) — Boston Teacher Residency graduates were initially less effective in math, caught up by roughly year three and outperformed by years four to five, with ELA effects small and imprecise, alongside greater racial diversity, more high-need placements, and stronger district retention. The paper's rendering of that study is accurate. I am less confident about the precise findings of the REL reports (Terziev & Forde 2021; Wan et al. 2021), the Sloan/New Visions evaluations, and the effectiveness results in Silva et al. (2014); my flags on those are "verify at the source," not asserted errors. I have moderate confidence that An & Koedel's Kansas City value-added estimates are larger than this paper's, which is why I frame that as something to check rather than a confirmed mischaracterization.

On the missing staggered-DiD citations specifically: the absence of Callaway & Sant'Anna (2021) and Sun & Abraham (2021) is not a substantive problem. Both are covered by the Roth et al. (2023) synthesis the paper does cite, they belong to the same family as the two estimators the paper actually runs (Borusyak imputation and de Chaisemartin group-time), and the robustness table in Table A3 already demonstrates the sensitivity that adding them would demonstrate. Readers should not treat this as a gap. The econometrics gap that does matter is on the inference side rather than the estimation side — pre-trend test power and few-treated-cluster standard errors — because the paper's substantive conclusions turn on marginal p-values and on parallel-trends tests it treats as informative evidence.

One structural observation about how the review is deployed. The literature review is genuinely balanced, but the discussion applies it slightly asymmetrically: where the paper finds nulls (diversity, retention), it foregrounds the multi-program literature that also found nulls and frames the earlier positive single-program findings as artifacts of selection; where it finds positive effects (effectiveness, high-need endorsements), it foregrounds the supportive single-program literature. Each move is individually defensible and the paper is honest enough that a reader can see both, but the net effect is that prior evidence is treated as more credible when it agrees. This is worth holding in mind, particularly because the paper's diversity null and its effectiveness positive have similar statistical support but very different rhetorical treatment.

On positioning in the broader field: the paper sits at the intersection of teacher preparation program evaluation and the economics of teacher labor markets, and it is much better connected to the first than to the second. The recruitment/diversity and effectiveness sections read as fully situated. The employment, retention, and especially mobility sections read as a set of administrative-data outcomes analyzed without the labor-market theory that would tell a reader what to expect or how to interpret a move. Given that mobility is the finding the paper flags as "somewhat surprising" and that it appears in the abstract, this is the place where an informed reader most needs to bring outside literature to the table.

Finally, on novelty overall: the claim that this is a methodological step beyond prior residency work is fair and I would defend it. No prior study I am aware of exploits within-program variation in residency adoption, and the effort to validate a self-reported treatment against independently collected Title II clinical-hours data is a real methodological contribution that other researchers studying program-model change could reuse. The oversell is narrow and localized to the "strongest evidence yet" phrasing about effectiveness in the final paragraph; the rest of the paper's self-positioning is, if anything, unusually modest.

---

### Writing Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

This is a clearly organized, unusually self-critical paper whose prose generally tracks its exhibits and whose hedging ("suggestive," "may," an explicitly pre-announced p<.1 convention) is more honest than most. But several genuine text–table disagreements survived production — a swapped earlier/later-adopter split, a 23-vs-15 rubric-item contradiction that determines a headline effect-size benchmark, and an arithmetic error in Table 1 — and a nontrivial share of the paper's most affirmative claims (special education, partner-district mobility, relocation quality) appear only in prose with no exhibit behind them. Readers can trust the architecture of the argument but should verify individual numbers before quoting them.

**Strengths:**

- Organization is genuinely good and the load-bearing material is easy to locate: the treatment-validation exercise (Table 2 + Figure 1) is placed at the end of Methods rather than buried in an appendix, so a reader encounters the evidence that "reported adoption" means something real before encountering any outcome estimate. The "Considerations in Interpreting Effects" subsection collects the external-validity argument in one place instead of scattering it.
- The paper pre-announces its interpretive conventions rather than smuggling them in. It states outright (Methods, Interpretation) that imprecision means it will "discuss results for which p < .1, classifying these as marginally statistically significant" and will lean on event-study face validity and robustness. A reader knows the rules of the game before the results start.
- Limitations are stated early, repeatedly, and specifically — the reliance on 15 identifying programs, the exclusion of the 13 always-residencies (including 5 pre-2011 adopters and 8 born-as-residencies), the undergraduate skew, and the retrospective self-report treatment measure all appear in the abstract-adjacent intro, in Methods, and again in Discussion. This is well above the field norm.
- Most quoted numbers do check out. Every summary statistic in the Sample paragraph matches Table 1 (90.7% White vs 0.09 racial minority; 18.3% high-need vs 0.18; 58.7% employed vs 0.59; 29.4% partner district vs 0.29; 10.6% left vs 0.11; 14.7% moved schools vs 0.15, "mostly to new districts" vs 0.10). The 3.7 pp / 25.7% high-need claim, the 2.6 pp / 18.2% and 1.2 pp / 13.3% mobility claims, and the 95.9-hour Title II claim all reconcile against Table 3, Table 2, and the Table 1 "Pre" column baselines. All four significance legends (Tables 2, 3, A1, A3, A4) match the stars actually used, including Table 3, whose legend correctly omits ** because no ** appears.
- Table and figure notes are unusually informative. The Table 1 note explains the otherwise baffling Pre=19 / Post=15 program counts (four programs adopted in 2019–2020 and are observed only pre-transition, so 34+19+13=66 reconciles), and both figure notes warn that pre-trend coefficients and treatment effects come from separate regressions with an unconventional reference category.
- Effect sizes are benchmarked against something interpretable (novice-teacher experience gains) rather than left as bare coefficients, and the paper openly says the observation-rating benchmark is the weaker of the two.

**Weaknesses:**

- Direct text–table contradiction on the adopter split. The Robustness Checks section says the sample was split into "earlier (up through 2015–2016, N = 9) and later-adopting (in 2016–2017 or after, N = 6) programs." The Table A4 note says the opposite: "Earlier adopters are those (N = 6) who adopted the residency model prior to the 2016–2017 school year; later adopters are those (N = 9) who adopted in 2016–2017 or after." The cutoff agrees; the counts are swapped. Worse, the very next sentence in the text introduces a third description — "a rosier picture of impacts for the six programs adopting the model in the 2013–2014 and 2014–2015 school years" — which contradicts its own "up through 2015–2016, N = 9" one sentence earlier and instead matches the table note's N=6. A reader cannot determine from the paper how many programs sit in either Table A4 column.
- Direct internal contradiction on the observation rubric, and it is load-bearing. Methods states annual observation scores are constructed "by averaging across all 23 rubric items for each observed lesson." The Discussion converts the OR estimate into "an average increase of about half a point on 1 of 15 indicators on the state rubric." Both cannot be right, and the arithmetic reveals which one the benchmark used: 0.5/15 = 0.033, matching the 0.032 estimate, while 0.5/23 = 0.022 does not. If the Methods figure of 23 is correct, the Discussion's headline interpretation of the observation-rating effect overstates it by roughly 50%.
- Arithmetic error in Table 1. The "In-state" row reports All = 22,384, but the four subgroup columns sum to 22,304 (8,034 + 7,611 + 4,347 + 2,312). Every other row in Table 1 sums correctly, and the Never+Pre+Post subtotal of 19,992 matches the In-state N in Table A2 exactly — so the column entries are right and the "All" cell is an 80-observation typo. Trivial substantively, but it is the kind of thing that tells a reader the table was not fully proofed.
- Several of the paper's most affirmative claims have no exhibit. The special-education result ("2.9 pp, 20.4% over a baseline of 14.2%, p = .019") — the single statistically significant recruitment finding, promoted to the Discussion and to the closing paragraph — is reported only in prose; there is no subject-area disaggregation table anywhere. The same is true of the entire partner-district mobility analysis ("Compellingly, we find that adopting the model reduces the district mobility of graduates working in partner districts... by 2.3 pp, p = .004... 1.2 pp, p < .001"), the school-characteristic difference-score analyses (suspension rates, demographics, achievement), and the covariate-robustness check, which the text itself labels "analyses not reported here." A reader who wants to evaluate these cannot.
- The special-education baseline is internally puzzling. The paper reports a pre-treatment special-education baseline of 14.2% against a pre-treatment all-high-need baseline of 14.4% (implied by 0.037/0.257, and matching Table 1's Pre column of 0.14). Taken literally, this means science, math, foreign language, and ESL endorsements combined account for roughly 0.2 percentage points — implausible unless endorsements are non-exclusive or the two baselines are computed on different denominators. Neither is explained, and the discrepancy is invisible unless a reader does the division.
- An unflagged parallel-trends violation on a headline outcome. Table 3 reports a Wald test for candidate diversity of F51 = 2.745, p = .022 — a clearer violation than the ELA VAM test (p = .079) the text does flag, and comparable to the school-mobility test (p = .010) it flags. The text never mentions it, yet the abstract's first substantive claim ("We generate skepticism that any improvements in diversity... stem from this transition") and a full Discussion paragraph rest on that outcome. The later characterization of "unconditional parallel pre-trends for most outcomes" is technically true but lets the reader assume the exceptions are the ones already named.
- The abstract's two affirmative findings sit on the two outcomes with the worst pre-trend diagnostics. "Suggestive evidence that adoption may increase the instructional effectiveness" rests on ELA VAM alone (p = .085 first year, p = .061 all years; math VAM and observation ratings are null), the same outcome whose Wald test is marginally violated at p = .079. "Somewhat surprisingly — the likelihood of migration across schools and districts" rests on moved schools, whose Wald test fails at p = .010 and which the Results text itself says warrants "some caution." The abstract carries none of that caution.
- The robustness narrative undersells one adverse column. Table A3's traditional two-way fixed-effects column turns moved schools (0.020) and moved districts (0.006) statistically insignificant — the mobility finding the abstract advertises does not survive the conventional estimator — and turns candidate diversity marginally negative (−0.016+), i.e., faint evidence that adoption reduced diversity. Neither is mentioned; the text concludes "For the most part, though, our takeaways are largely unchanged." Relatedly, the Methods claim to be "presenting the more conservative estimates obtained via our preferred estimator" holds against de Chaisemartin–D'Haultfoeuille but not against plain TWFE for mobility (0.026 vs 0.020) or observation ratings (0.032 vs 0.008).
- The closing paragraph's "some of the strongest evidence yet" trades on an ambiguity. The authors plainly mean strongest in design — first credibly causal, statewide, multi-program. Most readers will hear strongest in finding. What the sentence is actually built on is one marginal p-value out of three effectiveness measures, a mobility result with a violated pre-trend that vanishes under TWFE, and an endorsement result whose aggregate is p = .233. The policy sentence that follows — "it may pay dividends in elevating early-career teaching quality" — is the line most likely to be extracted and quoted, and it is the least supported sentence in the paper.
- The "lower bounds" frame is asserted, not demonstrated, and is applied asymmetrically. It appears in Methods, in Note 2, and twice in Discussion, and it invites the reader to treat every null as an underestimate of a real effect. Attenuation from treatment misclassification would shrink the positive ELA and mobility estimates too, but the frame is deployed mainly to defend nulls and to argue the true effects are larger.
- Some conditioning and labeling is carried in prose only. Mobility outcomes are conditional on retention and partner-district employment is conditional on employment (stated once in Methods, visible only as shrinking Ns), but Table 3 Panel C simply reads "Moved schools" / "Moved districts." Table 1's row "Ever found employment" is governed by a note restricting all outcomes to the year immediately after graduation, so the label and the note pull in opposite directions; the same label reappears in Table 3 under a column explicitly labeled "First year only." And Table 3's two columns differ by nearly sevenfold in N (12,812 vs 83,943) with only a single bottom row to explain why.
- Minor overstatements against the exhibits. "Graduates of always-residencies tend to have the highest rates of employment... mobility, and instructional effectiveness" — true for observation ratings (3.56) and math VAM (0.01), but the Always ELA VAM (−0.03) is below the Never column (−0.01). "For nearly all outcomes, estimates obtained following de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille are larger" — true for six or seven of ten, not nearly all. "Estimates of effects that are later to emerge... are slightly reduced" describes an observation-rating estimate that falls from 0.032 to 0.008, a 75% reduction. And the survey-coverage figures (72.9% of programs, 84.2% of graduates) cannot be reconciled with the reported 66 programs and 24,625 graduates against Table A1's 27,968 population (which implies 88.0%); the windows and exclusions may differ, but nothing in the paper lets a reader close the gap.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Read in this order if time-constrained: Table 1 (especially the Pre/Post/Always columns and the note about the four 2019–2020 adopters) → the Methods subsection "Interpretation" → Table 2 with Figure 1 → Table 3 → the Discussion's "Considerations in Interpreting Effects." The Literature Review and "The Teacher Residency Model" opening sections are competent background and can be skimmed by anyone who knows the residency literature.
- Read Endnote 9 before you look at Figures 1 and 2. It contains the single most important piece of interpretive guidance in the paper: with the Borusyak estimator, pre-trends and treatment effects come from separate regressions with different reference categories, so "a violation of the parallel trends assumption looks more like a line with some non-zero slope that starts at or near zero rather than one that ends at zero at t − 1." Reading these event studies with ordinary event-study habits will mislead you.
- Table 3 is the paper. Table 2 is the second-most important exhibit — it is the paper's answer to "does self-reported adoption mean anything?", and the honest answer it gives (23.7 pp on prioritizing district needs, but only 5.9 pp on yearlong placement and ~96 Title II hours against the ~500 a real semester-to-year shift implies) is what justifies reading every headline result as a diluted-treatment estimate. Do not skip it to get to the results.
- Read the Wald tests embedded in the row labels of Tables 2 and 3, not just the coefficients — they are the parallel-trends diagnostics and they are easy to skim past. Three of ten Table 3 outcomes fail at p < .1: candidate diversity (p = .022), moved schools (p = .010), and ELA VAM (p = .079). The text flags the latter two and is silent on the first. Note also that Table 3's note says the Wald tests are for column 1 only — column 2's pre-trends are never tested or reported.
- Do not quote the earlier/later adopter counts. The Robustness Checks text (earlier N = 9, later N = 6) and the Table A4 note (earlier N = 6, later N = 9) directly contradict each other, and the same text sentence contains a third, narrower description ("the six programs adopting the model in the 2013–2014 and 2014–2015 school years"). The substantive pattern in Table A4 is internally coherent and matches the Discussion — larger high-need and observation-rating effects in the "Earlier" column, larger VAM effects in the "Later" column — so cite the direction if you must, but not the program counts.
- If you cite the observation-rating effect size, check the rubric denominator yourself. Methods says scores average 23 rubric items; the Discussion's "half a point on 1 of 15 indicators" benchmark only works with 15. Use the raw estimate (0.032 points on a five-point scale, statistically indistinguishable from zero) rather than the verbal benchmark.
- Treat four claims as unverifiable from the published exhibits: the special-education endorsement result (2.9 pp, p = .019), the partner-district mobility results (2.3 pp, p = .004 and 1.2 pp, p < .001), the school-characteristic difference-score analyses (the suspension-rate finding), and the covariate-inclusion robustness check. None appears in any table or figure. The special-education claim in particular carries a baseline (14.2%) that is essentially identical to the all-high-need baseline (14.4%), which the paper never explains.
- If you cite the mobility finding, cite Table A3 alongside Table 3. It is the abstract's most eye-catching result, it has the paper's worst pre-trend diagnostic (p = .010), and it loses statistical significance under traditional two-way fixed effects (0.020, ns for schools; 0.006, ns for districts) — a fact the robustness narrative does not surface.
- Read the abstract as design-strong, evidence-weak. Its nulls (diversity, employment, retention) are the paper's most defensible contribution and are the right thing to cite. Its two affirmative clauses rest on marginal p-values on the two outcomes with flagged pre-trends, and its hedges ("suggestive," "may") are load-bearing — do not drop them in a citation.
- When the Discussion says "some of the strongest evidence yet," substitute "the most credibly identified evidence yet." That is what the design earns and what the authors almost certainly mean. The findings themselves are one marginal ELA VAM coefficient and a pre-trend-compromised mobility result; the strength claim is about identification, not about magnitude or precision.
- Treat the "lower bounds" framing as an interpretive argument rather than an established property. It appears four times and is genuinely plausible given the diluted first stage in Table 2, but it is never bounded or quantified, and the same attenuation logic would shrink the paper's positive estimates as well as its nulls.
- Mind the conditional denominators. Mobility is estimated among employed graduates who did not leave, and partner-district employment among the employed — stated once in Methods and otherwise visible only in the falling Ns (22,099 → 12,812 → 11,454). Table 1's "Ever found employment" row is likewise governed by a note restricting it to the first post-graduation year, so the 0.59 is a first-year rate despite the label.
- Table A1 is worth five minutes but not more trust than it deserves. It supports the external-validity argument, but its "comparability" rests on nulls in an underpowered program-clustered comparison — the racial-minority gap (−.043 on a 0.136 base, roughly a third) is null but far from small — and the one large significant difference (undergraduate, +35 pp) is described in the text only as "disproportionately composed of undergraduate programs."

**Detailed Commentary:**

Overall character of the writing. This is a well-built paper at the paragraph and section level. The argument has a clear spine: prior residency evidence is confounded by program-level differences and single-program samples; a within-program design over a statewide panel can separate the model from the programs that adopt it; here is what that design finds; here is why the finding is a lower bound. Each section does its job, headings are informative, and the authors reliably tell you what an exhibit is going to show before showing it. Sentences are long and heavily subordinated, so the paper reads slowly, but not obscurely. The unusual structural choice — putting the treatment-validation exercise (Table 2, Figure 1) at the close of Methods rather than in the appendix — is the right one and should be preserved in any reader's mental map, since it is what licenses the diluted-treatment reading of everything downstream.

Where the prose is most trustworthy. The descriptive passages are clean. Every figure in the Sample paragraph reconciles against Table 1, and the derived percentage changes in Results all reconcile against the Table 1 "Pre" column (3.7/14.4 = 25.7%; 2.6/14.3 = 18.2%; 1.2/9.0 = 13.3%), even though the paper never states that the Pre column is the denominator. Reported p-values reconcile against the displayed coefficient/SE ratios throughout Tables 2 and 3, including the two ELA VAM values (p = .084 and p = .059) and the Title II clinical-hours estimate (95.90/35.67 → p = .007). The Table 1 program-count arithmetic works once the note about the four 2019–2020 adopters is applied (34 + 19 + 13 = 66; 19 = 15 + 4), and 15/66 = 22.7% as claimed. The Table 1 subgroup Ns reconcile against the Table 3 and Table A2 analytic Ns row by row. The mobility decomposition holds: 2.6 pp school moves minus 1.2 pp district moves leaves 1.4 pp within-district, so "evenly split between movement within and across districts" is exactly right. All five significance legends match the stars actually printed. This is a paper that was checked — which makes the places where checking failed more informative, not less.

Where it fails. Three hard errors survived production. The earlier/later adopter counts are swapped between the Robustness text and the Table A4 note, and the text is additionally inconsistent with itself across two consecutive sentences ("up through 2015–2016, N = 9" followed by "the six programs adopting the model in the 2013–2014 and 2014–2015 school years"). The rubric-item count is 23 in Methods and 15 in the Discussion, and the Discussion's arithmetic only works with 15, which means the paper's verbal interpretation of the observation-rating magnitude is anchored to a number its own Methods section contradicts. And Table 1's In-state "All" cell (22,384) does not equal its own column sum (22,304), a fact confirmed by Table A2's In-state N of 19,992, which matches the Never+Pre+Post subtotal exactly.

The larger fidelity issue is selective emphasis rather than misreporting. Nothing in this paper is fabricated, and the authors hedge more than most. But three patterns systematically push the reader toward the positive reading. First, the parallel-trends diagnostics are reported for every outcome yet discussed only where they are convenient: the ELA VAM (p = .079) and school-mobility (p = .010) violations are flagged in the text, while candidate diversity (p = .022) — a larger violation than the first — is never mentioned, even though the abstract's lead claim is about diversity. Second, the robustness discussion characterizes the traditional TWFE column as leaving "takeaways largely unchanged" when that column in fact nullifies the mobility result the abstract advertises and produces a marginally significant negative diversity estimate.
