Third, the "lower bounds" framing, repeated four times, converts every null into evidence of an undetected effect while never being applied to the positive estimates it would equally attenuate.

The abstract and the closing paragraph. The abstract is more careful than the closing paragraph. It correctly leads with skepticism about diversity, employment, and retention — the paper's real contribution — and marks its two affirmative claims as "suggestive." What it omits is that both affirmative claims land on the two outcomes whose pre-trend tests are compromised, and that "instructional effectiveness" means ELA value-added alone, with math VAM and observation ratings null. The Discussion's final paragraph is where rhetoric most outruns evidence: "we provide some of the strongest evidence yet that model adoption may drive changes in graduates' instructional effectiveness" is a claim about design strength phrased as a claim about finding strength, and the policy sentence that closes the paper ("it may pay dividends in elevating early-career teaching quality") asks a p = .085 coefficient on 2,613 first-year observations, with a marginally violated pre-trend, to carry a recommendation. That is the sentence that will be quoted in policy briefs, and it is the one a reader should quote most cautiously.

Exhibits: what carries the argument. Table 3 is the paper. Table 2 with Figure 1 is the necessary companion — the honest first stage, showing that "became a residency" in this data means a 23.7 pp jump in prioritizing district needs, a 5.9 pp jump in yearlong placements, and roughly 96 additional Title II clinical hours against the ~500 a genuine semester-to-year shift implies. Table 1's Always column is what the external-validity argument rests on. Figure A1 is the visual map of the identifying variation and is worth thirty seconds. Table A3 matters more than its appendix placement suggests, because it is where the mobility finding weakens. Table A2 and Table A1 are supporting and can be skimmed. Figures 1 and 2 cannot be read correctly without Endnote 9.

What is missing from the exhibits entirely. The subject-area disaggregation behind the special-education result, the partner-district-by-mobility interaction analysis (the Discussion's most enthusiastic passage — "Compellingly, we find..."), the school-characteristic difference-score analyses, and the covariate-robustness check are all prose-only. Together these account for a meaningful share of the paper's affirmative content, and a reader has no way to assess specifications, samples, or multiple comparisons for any of them.

A caveat on this assessment. This review is based on a text extraction, so Figures 1, 2, and A1 were evaluated only through their notes and the prose describing them. Claims about axis scaling, visual legibility, and whether the event-study patterns actually look the way the text says they look could not be checked directly, and readers should verify the figures themselves — particularly since the paper explicitly asks them to lean on "the face validity offered by both the dynamic patterns of effects displayed in our event studies" in place of conventional significance thresholds.

---

### Contribution Review

**Rating:** Strong (moderate confidence)

This paper replaces the field's dominant research design for teacher residencies — comparing graduates of (usually one, usually exemplary) residency programs to other novice teachers in the same districts — with a within-program, staggered-adoption difference-in-differences built on a novel statewide survey that dates when each Tennessee preparation program began calling itself a residency. Its most durable contribution is a set of reasonably tight nulls on exactly the outcomes that anchor the policy case for residencies — racial diversity of graduates and retention in teaching — which credibly reattributes prior positive findings to program selection rather than the model itself. Its positive findings (instructional effectiveness, mobility, high-need endorsements) are much weaker than the abstract's phrasing implies, and the estimand is the effect of a mostly-undergraduate traditional program relabeling itself an at-least-"partial" residency, not the effect of the residency model as designed.

**Strengths:**

- Genuine design novelty with a clear identifying logic. Prior residency evaluations (An & Koedel 2021; Papay et al. 2012; Silva et al. 2014, 2015; Wan et al. 2021; Sloan & Blazevski 2015) compare residency graduates to other early-career teachers, leaving program-level confounders — selectivity, reputation, cost, location, faculty and curricular quality — fully in the estimate. Program fixed effects sweep all of those out. That is the single most important thing missing from this literature, and this is the first paper to supply it at scale.
- The treatment-timing measurement is itself a contribution. The retrospective survey (72.9% of programs, 84.2% of graduates) that dates adoption year-by-year, and the accompanying feature-by-feature timing questions, create a panel of program identity that did not previously exist. Figure A1 makes the identifying variation legible. This instrument is reusable and is arguably as citable as the estimates.
- The Table 2 "first stage" is unusually disciplined for this literature. Rather than assuming self-reported residency status means something, the authors run the same DiD with model features as outcomes, and then cross-validate against externally reported Title II clinical-hour and induction-hour data. Very few education-policy papers with a self-reported treatment do this. It converts an unverifiable label into a documented bundle of changes (+23.7pp district-needs recruitment priority, +5.9pp yearlong placement, +6.5pp financial incentives, +4.5pp mentor compensation, ~+96 clinical hours), and it is honest that this bundle is far short of full-model implementation.
- The nulls are the most valuable output and are informative, not just underpowered. Diversity: −0.013 (0.010), so the upper bound of the 95% interval is roughly +0.7pp against a ~7% pre-treatment base — an order of magnitude smaller than the diversity advantages reported for boutique residencies. Leaving teaching: 0.005 (0.009), ruling out reductions in first-year attrition larger than about 1.3pp on a ~10% base. Even after generous scaling for treatment dilution, these nulls do not accommodate the effect sizes the advocacy literature attributes to residencies. Notably, the parallel-trends test for the retention outcome is clean (p = .284).
- The paper draws its own boundaries with real candor: it names the 15-program identifying sample, the exclusion of all 13 always-residencies (including all seven externally certified by NCTR/TDOE), the undergraduate skew, the retrospective self-report, the imprecision, and the "lower bound" interpretation. The Table A1 responder/non-responder comparison and the Table A2 cohort-composition checks (supporting a preparation-channel rather than a recruitment-channel reading) are the right robustness exercises and are reported without spin.
- Two exploratory extensions are more useful than their brief treatment suggests: mobility is lower among graduates working in partner districts (−2.3pp, p = .004, statistically different from non-partner graduates at p < .001), and mobile graduates do not move toward whiter or higher-achieving schools. Together these defuse the most alarming reading of the mobility result and should travel with any citation of it.

**Weaknesses:**

- The estimand is not the residency model. Treatment is a program self-reporting "fully" or "partially" becoming a residency, and Table 2 shows the hallmark feature moved only 5.9pp (yearlong clinical placement) and ~96 of the ~500 clinical hours such a shift would imply. The paper's own footnote 2 concedes that some "transitions" may be partial-to-full moves. So the estimates are closer to an intent-to-treat on a heavily diluted, heterogeneous bundle plus a label change. "The teacher residency model has no effect on diversity" and "converting a traditional Tennessee undergraduate program into a self-described partial residency has no detectable effect on diversity" are different claims, and only the second is estimated here.
- The most quotable claim is the least supported. The abstract's "adoption may increase the instructional effectiveness" rests on ELA VAM = 0.031 (0.018), p = .084, on 2,613 observations from a measure covering only about a third of employed graduates — and the pre-trend Wald test for that same outcome is itself marginal (p = .079). The preferred-estimator math VAM is null (0.034, SE 0.024) and observation ratings are null (0.032, SE 0.033). The discussion's "some of the strongest evidence yet" for effectiveness effects is doing more work than one marginal coefficient with a marginal pre-trend violation can bear.
- The mobility finding — the paper's most surprising result — sits on an outcome whose parallel-trends test is rejected at p = .010 (moved schools). The authors flag this, but the discussion then builds two follow-up analyses and a policy narrative on top of it. Readers should treat "residency adoption increases graduate mobility" as a hypothesis generated here, not a result established here.
- An unflagged pre-trend problem sits under the headline null: candidate diversity has a Wald test of F(51) = 2.745, p = .022 — a rejection at conventional levels — and the text never discusses it, even while the paper carefully discusses the p = .010 and p = .079 violations elsewhere. Since the diversity null is the finding most likely to be cited against residency advocacy, the asymmetry in how pre-trend evidence is surfaced is a real limitation of the paper as a reference.
- The "lower bound" framing is in tension with the paper's own heterogeneity results. The argument is that earlier and always-residency adopters implement more faithfully, so full-fidelity effects should exceed these estimates. But Table A4 shows the effectiveness gains are driven by later adopters (math VAM 0.115*, ELA 0.080***) — precisely the group the authors elsewhere characterize as implementing the model least comprehensively. Either fidelity is not the mechanism behind the effectiveness result, or the result is a small-sample artifact; the paper does not resolve this, and the lower-bound claim should not be cited as if it were established.
- The identifying sample is thin and non-random in a way that matters for exactly the outcomes at issue. Fifteen programs, disproportionately undergraduate; the 13 always-residencies (which Table 1 shows have 24% teachers of color vs. 5-10% elsewhere, and the strongest employment and effectiveness outcomes) contribute nothing. The paper is transparent about this, but it means the design's internal-validity gain is purchased by excluding the very programs the policy conversation is actually about.
- A reporting inconsistency in the heterogeneity analysis: the text describes earlier adopters as those through 2015-16 with N = 9 and later adopters as N = 6 (and the discussion refers to "the six programs adopting the model in the 2013-2014 and 2014-2015 school years"), while the Table A4 note reverses this (earlier N = 6, later N = 9). Readers citing the cohort-heterogeneity results should treat the group definitions as unverified.
- Tennessee's graduate pool is 90.7% White, and the authors themselves note that undergraduate enrollment decisions are made years before program completion. The diversity null is therefore doubly setting-bound: it is a null about whether an existing, mostly-White undergraduate institution can diversify its own teacher-candidate pipeline by relabeling its preparation program — a narrower and less surprising question than whether the residency model can build a diverse teaching corps.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Cite it for: the design. This is now the reference for the point that cross-program comparisons of residency and non-residency graduates cannot separate the model from the program, and for a workable alternative (within-program staggered DiD on survey-dated adoption, with a documented first stage). That methodological argument is the paper's most transferable contribution.
- Cite it for: skepticism about the diversity claim. "When existing traditional programs adopt the residency model, graduates do not become more racially diverse" is well supported — the estimate is a tight null (−1.3pp, SE 1.0pp) that survives dilution scaling and is consistent with the multi-program literature (Matsko et al. 2022; Terziev & Forde 2021; Wan et al. 2021). Pair the citation with the caveat that this outcome's own parallel-trends test is rejected at p = .022 and that Tennessee's candidate pool is 90.7% White.
- Cite it for: the retention null. 0.005 (0.009) on leaving teaching, with a clean pre-trend test (p = .284), replicated across estimators and across first-year and all-year specifications. This is the cleanest estimate in the paper and directly contradicts the retention rationale that appears in federal residency funding arguments.
- Cite it for: the descriptive finding that self-described residency adoption in practice means a modest bundle — mostly a stronger recruitment orientation toward district staffing needs, plus roughly 96 extra clinical hours — rather than a wholesale conversion to the model. Table 2 is the best available evidence on what the residency label actually denotes at scale, and it is a useful corrective to policy documents that treat "residency" as a fixed treatment.
- Do not lean on it for: "residencies improve instructional effectiveness." The claim rests on one marginally significant ELA VAM coefficient (p = .084) whose own pre-trend test is marginal (p = .079), with null math VAM and null observation ratings under the preferred estimator, and effects driven by the least-faithful adopters. Anyone citing this direction should quote the coefficient and its caveats, not the abstract sentence.
- Do not lean on it for: "residencies increase teacher mobility." The p = .010 pre-trend violation on that outcome undermines the counterfactual, and the sign of the welfare interpretation is unresolved — the paper's own follow-ups show mobility falls for graduates placed in partner districts.
- Do not lean on it for: "the residency model does not work." The design deliberately excludes every always-residency in the state, including all seven externally certified ones, and the treatment contrast is a partial conversion. The paper estimates the return to a marginal, mostly-undergraduate program relabeling itself, which is a policy-relevant but distinctly narrower question.
- Do not lean on it for: "these are lower bounds on full-model effects." That interpretation is asserted, not demonstrated, and it is contradicted by the Table A4 pattern in which later (less faithful) adopters drive the effectiveness estimates.
- Open questions a reader should know remain unresolved: (1) whether full-fidelity or externally certified residencies produce the outcomes attributed to them — the always-residency programs are still evaluable only by the confounded cross-program design this paper criticizes; (2) whether graduate-level residencies, where the model is more commonly implemented and where recruitment can plausibly be reshaped, behave differently from the undergraduate programs identified here; (3) dose-response — which specific features (clinical length, mentor quality, financial incentives) drive any effects, which this design cannot separate; (4) whether the mobility result replicates under a design with credible pre-trends, and whether increased mobility reflects better job-market matching or weaker district attachment; (5) whether partner-district employment effects emerge over a longer horizon than the first post-graduation year; (6) whether the diversity null holds in states with more racially diverse college-going populations.
- Read it alongside: Truwit, Ronfeldt & Bardelli (2024, AERA Open) on what residencies in Tennessee actually implement, which supplies the implementation-fidelity context that makes this paper's estimand interpretable; and An & Koedel (2021) and Papay et al. (2012) for the boutique-program benchmarks this paper is arguing against. The two literatures now answer different questions and should be cited as such rather than as competing estimates of the same parameter.

**Detailed Commentary:**

How the field should update. Before this paper, the empirical case for teacher residencies rested almost entirely on comparisons between graduates of a small number of well-regarded, often standalone programs and other novice teachers hired into the same districts. That design cannot distinguish the model from the programs implementing it, and the pattern in the literature — favorable results in single-program studies, weaker or absent results in multi-program studies — is exactly what selection would produce. Truwit and Ronfeldt supply the missing counterfactual and find that the two claims doing the most work in residency advocacy, diversity and retention, do not survive it. That is a meaningful update: it shifts the burden of proof onto proponents to show that the model, rather than the programs, produces those outcomes, and it does so with nulls precise enough to be informative rather than merely uninformative.

What the paper does not establish. The design's power comes at a steep price in scope. All identifying variation comes from 15 mostly-undergraduate programs that converted mid-panel; the 13 programs that were always residencies — including every externally certified one, and the ones Table 1 shows have the most diverse cohorts and strongest outcomes — are structurally excluded. And the treatment is a self-report of at least partial adoption whose measured content (Table 2) is modest: a 5.9pp increase in the probability of a yearlong clinical placement and about 96 additional clinical hours against the roughly 500 a genuine semester-to-year conversion implies. The honest description of the estimand is: what happens to graduate outcomes when a traditional Tennessee teacher preparation program, mostly undergraduate, begins to describe itself as a residency and makes a corresponding partial set of programmatic changes. That is a real and policy-relevant question — it is close to the decision a program leader contemplating adoption actually faces — but it is not the effect of the residency model as designed, and the paper's title question ("the model itself or something else?") is more sweeping than what the data can adjudicate.

The gap between the quotable and the supported. The abstract's two positive claims are its weakest results. "Adoption may increase the instructional effectiveness" rests on ELA value-added of 0.031 (SE 0.018, p = .084) on 2,613 observations, with a marginal pre-trend violation (p = .079) on that same outcome, null math VAM and null observation ratings under the preferred estimator, and — per Table A4 — effects concentrated among later adopters, the group the authors elsewhere characterize as implementing the model least faithfully. The mobility result carries a p = .010 pre-trend rejection. Both will nonetheless be the sentences that get cited, because they are the affirmative findings in a paper otherwise composed of nulls. Readers should invert the paper's rhetorical emphasis: the nulls are the contribution; the positives are hypotheses.

One asymmetry worth naming. The paper carefully surfaces the pre-trend problems attached to its positive findings but does not discuss the p = .022 parallel-trends rejection on candidate diversity — its headline null, and the estimate most likely to be cited in policy debate. A null with a rejected pre-trend is not thereby wrong, but it deserves the same treatment as the positives. This does not overturn the diversity conclusion, which is corroborated by the multi-program literature and by the plausible mechanism the authors describe (undergraduate enrollment decisions predate the transition by years), but it should accompany the citation.

Standing. On its actual question — what a traditional program should expect from converting — this is now the best available evidence, and there is no close competitor. On the broader question of whether well-implemented residencies deliver on diversity, retention, and effectiveness, the evidence base has not really advanced: that question still belongs to the descriptive, selection-prone literature this paper criticizes, and the programs best positioned to answer it are precisely the ones this design must drop. The most valuable thing the paper sets up is a template for the follow-on work: apply the same survey-dated, within-program design in states with more racially diverse candidate pipelines and more graduate-level adopters, and pair it with a dose-response specification on the individual model features rather than the residency label. Until that exists, the field's fair summary is that relabeling a traditional undergraduate program as a residency buys little on diversity and retention, may buy something modest on early-career effectiveness and high-need certifications, and that whether the fully implemented model does more remains genuinely unknown.

---

### Reproducibility Review

**Rating:** Weak (high confidence)

The paper names its data sources precisely and is unusually disciplined about internal sample accounting — every analytic N in Tables 2–3 reconciles exactly with Table 1 once the always-residency programs are removed — but it carries no data availability statement, no replication package, no posted code, and no statement of the software or estimation package used. Critically, the treatment variable comes from an author-administered survey that exists nowhere outside the authors' files, and neither the survey instrument nor any pathway for obtaining it or the Tennessee Department of Education administrative data is documented. Several of the paper's more striking claims — the special-education endorsement result, and both exploratory mobility follow-ups — appear only in prose with no table, no standard errors, and no sample sizes, and one sensitivity analysis is explicitly labeled "not reported here."

**Strengths:**

- Data sources are named with real specificity: the TDOE completer file (2009-10 to 2018-19), personnel data through 2020-21, evaluation data through 2019-20, TVAAS (with a link to SAS technical documentation at tvaas.sas.com), and U.S. Department of Education Title II files. The last of these is genuinely public, so Panel B of Table 2 is the one analysis a reader could attempt independently.
- Sample accounting is fully auditable from the printed tables. Table 1 reports N for every variable by program group, and every analytic N in Tables 2, 3, A2, A3, and A4 equals the Table 1 total minus the "Always" column (e.g., 24,625 − 2,526 = 22,099; 14,456 − 1,644 = 12,812; 11,419 − 1,044 = 10,375; 2,735 − 335 = 2,400). This lets a reader verify — though the text never states it outright — that the 13 always-residency programs are dropped rather than merely absorbed by fixed effects, and confirms the 13.8% alternative-certification exclusion is applied before all of it.
- The treatment-timing structure is shown, not just described: Figure A1 displays a program-by-year heatmap of self-identified residency status for all 66 programs, so the staggered adoption pattern (and the counts of 34 never / 15 transitioning / 13 always, plus the 4 programs adopting in 2019-20 observed only pre-transition) is visually inspectable and, in principle, partially digitizable.
- The estimator is cited exactly (Borusyak et al., 2024), clustering is stated in every table note ("standard errors clustered by program"), and note 9 is an unusually careful piece of methodological documentation: it explains that pre-trend and treatment-effect coefficients come from two separate regressions, that the placebo reference category is all untreated periods before the earliest specified effect plus never-treated observations rather than t−1, and it reports a pseudo-panel equivalence check (collapsing to program × year with weights equal to the number of non-missing contributing outcomes) that returns identical estimates and standard errors.
- Measurement limitations are documented in the footnotes at a level that many papers omit: observation-rating coverage rates by cohort (86.1% overall; 75.7% for 2016-17 completers vs. 93.2% for 2017-18, note 5), the absence of 2011-12 ORs and 2019-20 VAMs, the 2015-16 testing suspension, and the two assumptions embedded in the monotone treatment indicator (note 2).
- The paper is candid about what it did not do: the controls sensitivity check is openly labeled "analyses not reported here," the Title II year-alignment problem is flagged as unresolved (notes 11-12), and the exploratory difference-score analyses are explicitly described as underpowered and limited by school-characteristic coverage ending in 2017-18.

**Weaknesses:**

- There is no data availability statement anywhere in the article. The Acknowledgments thank TDOE for "partnership, support, and data" and carry the standard TDOE non-endorsement disclaimer, but no data-use agreement, application process, contact point, or restricted-access pathway is described. A reader who wanted the administrative data has no stated route to follow.
- No replication package, posted code, or repository is referenced — not even "available upon request." Journal-era norms for an EEPA article would expect a deposited package or a stated reason there is none.
- No software environment or estimation package is reported. The paper never says whether Stata, R, or something else was used, and never names the routine implementing Borusyak et al. (2024) — did_imputation is the obvious candidate, but it is not stated, nor is the de Chaisemartin–D'Haultfoeuille implementation (did_multiplegt vs. did_multiplegt_dyn, which give different answers). Table A3's robustness comparison therefore cannot be reproduced with confidence even by someone holding the data.
- The survey is the study's treatment variable and it is entirely private. Only the wording of the first item is quoted; the follow-up adoption-year item and the seven feature items are named but not reproduced (readers learn only incidentally, from note 12, that the clinical-length item is a binary indicator for placements longer than 8 months). The instrument is not in the appendix, not referenced as supplemental material, and no statement addresses whether it can be obtained. Without it, no one can rebuild the treatment indicator — which means the central estimates are not independently verifiable by anyone, with or without TDOE access.
- The unit of analysis "program" is never defined operationally. Table 1 shows that individual programs contain both undergraduate and graduate completers (e.g., "Never" programs are 66% undergraduate / 34% graduate), implying "program" means the provider or institution rather than a pathway. But the survey asked leaders about "your teacher preparation program," and the paper never says how a single response was applied to an institution offering multiple pathways, nor how the 66 programs map to Title II reporting units. Treatment assignment for multi-pathway institutions is therefore unrecoverable.
- The response-rate figures cannot be reconstructed from the reported numbers. 72.9% of programs and 84.2% of graduates imply roughly 90 programs statewide, but that total is never given; and Table A1's full comparison sample of 27,968 (alt-cert already excluded) against the analytic 24,625 implies 88.0% of non-alt-cert graduates, which does not obviously reconcile with 84.2% once the 13.8% alt-cert exclusion is applied to the denominator. A replicator cannot confirm they have assembled the same responding set.
- The Wald test degrees of freedom are uninterpretable as printed. Tables 2 and 3 report a single subscript (F51, F50, F49, F48, F47, F42) with an F-statistic and p-value, but a cluster-robust Wald test for parallel trends has both numerator and denominator degrees of freedom, and no p-value can be recovered from one number alone. The subscript varies across outcomes in a way that suggests it tracks the number of contributing program clusters, but this is a guess. Neither the number of pre-treatment placebo coefficients tested nor the event-window horizons (leads and lags, and whether endpoints are binned) is stated in the text — the figure notes reveal only that pre-trend references are "prior to t − 6." The parallel-trends diagnostics that the paper leans on to qualify its own results are thus not reproducible from the description.
- The two exploratory mobility follow-ups — the most reassuring findings in the Discussion — are reported in prose only. The partner-district subgroup analysis gives point estimates and p-values (−2.3 pp, p = .004; −1.2 pp, p < .001; between-group differences p < .001 and p = .012) but no standard errors, no sample sizes, no table, and no statement of how the subgroup interaction was specified within the imputation estimator (interacted treatment, split samples, or separate estimations). The difference-score analysis names no outcome variables beyond examples, reports no estimates at all, and states its conclusion ("null impacts on student demographics, achievement, attendance, and staff turnover; at most... lower suspension rates") with nothing a reader could check.
- The endorsement disaggregation is similarly table-free. The special-education result (2.9 pp, 20.4% over a 14.2% baseline, p = .019) and the "precise null" math and science estimates are asserted in text with no coefficients, standard errors, or Ns, even though the special-education finding carries substantial weight in the Discussion's policy framing.
- Column 2 of Table 3 (all available workforce years) has no reported parallel-trends diagnostics — the table note explicitly limits Wald tests to "first year only" — and no corresponding event studies, since Figure 2 covers first-year outcomes only. Several conclusions rest on Column 2 (persistence of mobility effects, the ELA VAM estimate at p = .059, the "fade-out" of effectiveness gains), and none of them can be assessed against a pre-trend.
- Two internal inconsistencies would force a replicator to guess. First, the observation-rating measure is described in the Methods as an average "across all 23 rubric items," but the Discussion translates the effect as "about half a point on 1 of 15 indicators on the state rubric" — and the arithmetic (0.032 × 15 ≈ 0.48) uses 15, so the outcome variable's construction and the headline effect-size interpretation disagree with each other. Second, the adoption-timing split is described three incompatible ways: the text says earlier adopters number 9 and later adopters 6, the Table A4 note says earlier N = 6 and later N = 9, and the text separately refers to "the six programs adopting the model in the 2013-2014 and 2014-2015 school years" as the earlier group while also placing the cutoff at "up through 2015-2016." The Table A4 column sample sizes do not settle which is right.
- The Title II year-alignment problem is acknowledged but left unresolved by the authors themselves. Note 11 states there is "some uncertainty as to whether certain data elements of 'Year t State Reports' correspond to year t or year t − 1," and note 12 attributes an observed timing discrepancy to that ambiguity — but the paper never says which convention it actually adopted. Since Title II is the only public input, this is precisely the analysis a reader could otherwise check, and the missing merge rule blocks it.
- No human-subjects statement appears. The survey collected data from program leaders with a \$20 incentive, but there is no mention of IRB review, consent, or confidentiality terms — which is also the most likely reason the program-level adoption data cannot be released, and would have been worth saying.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Treat the headline Table 3 estimates as credible but externally unverified. Nothing in the public record permits an independent check: the treatment variable exists only in the authors' survey files, and no access pathway is documented. Weight these results on the authors' credibility and the paper's internal coherence, not on their having been or being checkable.
- Weight the tabled results (Tables 2, 3, A2, A3, A4) considerably more heavily than the prose-only results. The special-education endorsement effect, the partner-district mobility reversal, and the school-characteristic difference scores are reported without standard errors, sample sizes, or specification detail, and none can be evaluated for power, multiple comparisons, or specification sensitivity. The partner-district finding in particular is doing real rhetorical work in the Discussion — it is the evidence offered that increased mobility is not a problem — and it is the least documented analysis in the paper.
- Before citing the Table A4 heterogeneity results, request clarification of which adopter cohort has N = 6 and which has N = 9. The text and the table note state opposite assignments, and a third passage describes the earlier group as six programs adopting in 2013-14 and 2014-15. As printed, a reader cannot tell whether the "later adopters drive the VAM effect" claim rests on six programs or nine.
- Ask the authors which software and which specific package and version implemented both the Borusyak et al. and de Chaisemartin–D'Haultfoeuille estimates, and what event-window horizons and binning were used. The Table A3 comparison across estimators — the paper's main defense of its estimator choice — turns on implementation details that are not stated, and the de Chaisemartin–D'Haultfoeuille routines have changed materially across versions.
- Do not treat the parallel-trends Wald tests as reproducible diagnostics. Request the numerator and denominator degrees of freedom, the number of placebo leads tested, and the event-window specification. This matters most for "Moved schools" (F48 = 3.186, p = .010), where the authors themselves say the test indicates a violation, and for ELA VAM (F42 = 2.145, p = .079) — the two results where the pre-trend evidence should most discipline interpretation.
- If you want to check anything independently, Panel B of Table 2 (Title II clinical and mentoring hours) is the only feasible target: those files are public. Before attempting it, ask the authors which year convention they used to merge "Year t State Reports," since notes 11-12 leave the alignment open and a one-year shift would change both the timing pattern in Figure 1 and the ~96-hour point estimate.
- Ask whether the survey instrument, the program-level adoption-year matrix underlying Figure A1, and the codebook for the 66-program roster can be released, and under what terms. The instrument is very likely shareable even if the linked administrative data are not, and it is the single document that would most improve the study's verifiability. A de-identified adoption-year table would also convert Figure A1 from a picture into usable data.
- Ask how "program" was defined for institutions offering multiple pathways, and how a single leader's response was propagated across pathways and degree levels. Table 1 shows programs spanning both undergraduate and graduate completers, so the answer determines whether treatment is measured at the right level — and it bears directly on the paper's own caveat that its estimates may not generalize to graduate pathways.
- Resolve the 23-versus-15 rubric-item discrepancy before quoting any effect-size benchmark for observation ratings. The Methods and Discussion disagree, and the "half a point on one indicator" translation depends entirely on which is correct.
- Request the unreported controls-sensitivity results described as "analyses not reported here." The claim that adding gender, elementary endorsement, in-state residence, prior experience, and prior achievement "does not meaningfully influence any of our estimates" supports the paper's central interpretive move — that effects reflect preparation rather than recruitment — and it is currently an assertion with no accompanying numbers.
- Note that this assessment is based on the article text as extracted; if the journal's online version carries a data availability statement, supplemental files, or an open-practices disclosure not present in the PDF body, check there before concluding nothing was deposited.

**Detailed Commentary:**

The right way to read this paper's reproducibility profile is that it is documented but not verifiable. Those are different things, and the paper is much better at the first than the second.

On documentation, Truwit and Ronfeldt are careful. The data sources are named at file level with their exact year coverage. The measurement caveats are footnoted with real numbers rather than gestured at — coverage rates for observation ratings by cohort, the specific years VAMs are missing and why, the two monotonicity assumptions behind the treatment indicator, the retroactive application of the 2020 partner-district requirement to all panel years (note 4). Note 9 explains the imputation estimator's two-regression structure and its unusual placebo reference category clearly enough that a reader who did not already know Borusyak et al. could correctly interpret Figures 1 and 2, and it reports a pseudo-panel equivalence check that most authors would not have bothered to run, let alone report. The sample accounting is the strongest element: every analytic N in the paper equals a Table 1 total minus the always-residency column, which means a careful reader can independently confirm the exclusion structure — the 13.8% alternative-certification drop, the removal of the 13 always-residency programs, and the outcome-specific attrition — without asking anyone anything.

On verifiability, the picture is quite different, and the binding constraint is not the restricted administrative data. Restricted data are a legitimate limitation and I do not hold their non-release against the paper. The binding constraint is that the treatment variable is a private instrument. The residency classification and adoption years come from a survey the authors designed and administered in 2019-20; nobody else has those responses, the instrument is not reproduced, and there is no statement about whether either could be obtained. Even a researcher sitting inside TDOE with full data access could not rebuild the key regressor. Combined with the absence of any data availability statement, any code, and any named software, this means no part of the central analysis has an independent verification path — not a hard one, not a slow one, none.

The specification is partially recoverable and partially not. The estimator is cited, the fixed effects are stated, clustering is stated, and note 9 clarifies the reference-period logic. But the event-window horizons are inferable only from the figures, the implementing package is unnamed, and the parallel-trends Wald tests are reported with a single degrees-of-freedom subscript that cannot support the printed p-values. Since the paper repeatedly and honestly uses those tests to discount its own findings — flagging the school-mobility violation at p = .010 and the ELA VAM pre-trend at p = .079 — the fact that they cannot be reconstructed is more consequential than it first appears. Readers are being asked to calibrate their trust using a diagnostic whose construction is opaque.

The sharpest reporting gap is the gradient between what got a table and what did not. The main estimates, the estimator comparison, the cohort heterogeneity, and the composition checks are all tabled with standard errors and Ns. But the special-education endorsement effect, the endorsement disaggregation, both exploratory mobility follow-ups, and the controls sensitivity are prose-only. This matters because those unreported analyses are not decorative. The partner-district subgroup result is the paper's answer to the most uncomfortable finding it reports — that becoming a residency increases graduate mobility — and it is stated as four p-values with no standard errors, no sample sizes, and no description of how the subgroup comparison was implemented inside an imputation estimator where subgroup interactions are non-trivial. A reader has no way to judge whether that analysis is well-powered, whether the p < .001 between-group difference survives clustering on 15 treated programs, or whether it was one of many cuts.

Two internal inconsistencies deserve flagging because they are the kind of thing a replicator hits immediately. The observation-rating outcome is built from 23 rubric items in the Methods but benchmarked against 15 indicators in the Discussion, with the arithmetic following the 15. And the adoption-timing split in Table A4 is described three mutually incompatible ways across text and table note. Neither is fatal to the paper's argument, but both are places where someone rebuilding the analysis would have to stop and guess, and the second one affects how a reader interprets the heterogeneity result.

Finally, the Title II analysis is worth singling out as a missed opportunity. It is the one input a reader could obtain freely, which makes Panel B of Table 2 the natural verification target. The authors themselves state in note 11 that they do not know whether "Year t State Reports" elements correspond to year t or t − 1, and in note 12 they attribute an observed timing discrepancy to exactly that ambiguity — but they never say which convention they used. That is unusually candid about a limitation and unusually unhelpful for verification at the same time. Naming the merge rule would have cost one sentence and made the corroboration analysis checkable.

Where this lands: "weak" rather than "adequate" because the combination of no data statement, no code, no software, no instrument, and no access pathway leaves the central results with zero independent verification route; and "weak" rather than "insufficient" because the paper is internally coherent, arithmetically auditable, and honest about its own limits to a degree that earns real credit. Readers should treat the tabled main effects as reasonable to cite with the authors' own caveats attached, and the prose-only exploratory findings as claims to hold at arm's length until the underlying numbers are available.
